modal_intro.title: The Astronomical Clock 🧭
modal_intro.headline: Welcome to the Astronomical Clock of St. Mary's
modal_intro.welcome: For more than 600 years, an astronomical clock has watched over the congregation of St. Mary's in Lübeck. This simulation invites you to explore this technical masterpiece up close — whether you're standing right in front of it or getting your first impression from home.
modal_intro.overview_text: Astronomical clocks like this one traditionally perform five tasks at once:
modal_intro.function_time: Using the hour hand, they tell the time.
modal_intro.function_astro: They display astronomical information: the moon phase and the positions of the sun and moon within the zodiac.
modal_intro.function_calendar: They provide calendar data — especially the kind needed to determine the movable feasts of the church year.
modal_intro.function_faith: As a furnishing of a house of worship, they make an iconographic statement about the relationship between God, the world, and humankind in Christianity.
modal_intro.function_art: And they are themselves an object of ecclesiastical and civic representation — artistically crafted by woodcarvers and painters.
modal_intro.dial_title: The Dial: A Sky in Motion
modal_intro.dial_text: This simulation recreates, with two hands and a rotating disc of stars, what the real clock at St. Mary's also shows: the movements of the sun, moon and zodiac — with remarkable precision.
modal_intro.dial_time: The sun hand completes exactly one rotation every 24 hours, showing the time on the replica Roman-numeral dial as it goes.
modal_intro.dial_sun_moon: The sun and moon hands display the actual astronomical positions of both bodies in the starry sky — not their fictitious astrological position.
modal_intro.dial_zodiac: The star disc completes one rotation every 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4.1 seconds and shows 13 constellations in their true, varying sizes — including the often-forgotten Ophiuchus between Scorpio and Sagittarius.
modal_intro.dial_moonphase: A small sphere, half golden, half dark, rolls along the moon hand. It completes one full rotation every 29.532 days — exactly one lunar month, since the moon hand takes 24 hours, 50 minutes and 28.2 seconds for its own orbit.
modal_intro.dial_center: At the centre of the dial, just as in the historical predecessor, sits the figure of the Saviour emerging from clouds and rays.
modal_intro.calendar_title: The Calendar Disc: Eight Rings of Time
modal_intro.calendar_text: The calendar disc is recreated in this simulation too: below the clock dial, it turns — carrying eight labelled rings from the outside in:
modal_intro.calendar_rings: Rings 1–4: day letters (A–G), month names, day numbers within each month, and the names of the church feast days.
modal_intro.calendar_year: Rings 5–7: the year ring covering the 170 years from 1911 to 2080, the Sunday letters, and the Golden Numbers from 1 to 19.
modal_intro.calendar_leap: Ring 8 shows the Easter dates. February 29th is automatically shown only in leap years — as a result, from March 1st onward all day letters are shifted by one step compared to medieval calendars.
modal_intro.calendar_eclipse: Since 1563, the Lübeck calendar disc has additionally recorded visible solar and lunar eclipses — a feature found on no other church clock in the Hanseatic region.
modal_intro.calendar_corners: The four corners are guarded by the symbols of the Evangelists: an angel for Matthew, a winged lion for Mark, a winged ox for Luke, and an eagle for John.
modal_intro.calendar_center: At the centre of the disc shines a sun with a human face.
modal_intro.figure_title: The Figure Superstructure: The Believers of the World
modal_intro.figure_note: This display of figures can only be experienced at the real clock in St. Mary's — the simulation does not recreate it.
modal_intro.figure_text: At the very top, in the clock's gable, a four-tiered arrangement of figures rises around the figure of Christ. It is not shown in this simulation.
modal_intro.figure_procession: At noon, a procession of eight figures from different parts of the world and cultures passes before Christ. Each figure bows, is blessed, and moves on — a symbol that his blessing extends to all people of the world.
modal_intro.figure_bell: Above the procession, an old man strikes the historic hour bell of 1721 with an hourglass in hand — a symbol of time.
modal_intro.figure_icons: Further figures around them speak of transience, and of past and future (as a double-headed Janus figure), of forgiveness and mercy, of humility, joy, faith and love — until Christ, right at the top, finally embodies Hope.
modal_intro.controls_text: You can control the simulation and retrieve important calendar information.
modal_intro.ctrl_sim_date: Enter a specific date between 01/01/1911 and 12/31/2080, along with a time.
modal_intro.ctrl_sim_now: Immediately resets the clock to the current system time.
modal_intro.ctrl_cal_data: Displays the calculated calendar data for the currently set date.
modal_intro.ctrl_cal_eclipse: Lists the solar and lunar eclipses for the currently set year (2000–2036).
modal_intro.ctrl_btn_cal: Explains how the day of the week can be determined.
modal_intro.ctrl_btn_hist: Provides background information on the history and restoration of the clock.
modal_intro.symbols_intro: To save space, the compact calendar overview uses symbols instead of spelled-out terms (details appear as a tooltip on tap/hover):
modal_intro.sources_text: Paul Behrens: "Die Astronomische Uhr in St. Marien", St.-Marien-Jahrbuch 1967, pp. 134–147. · Manfred Schukowski: "Die astronomische Uhr in der Lübecker Marienkirche", Astronomie + Raumfahrt 37 (2000) 4, pp. 34–36.

modal_calendar.title: The Calendar Disc
modal_calendar.intro: The calendar disc is divided into several circles. In the outer circle, alongside the 366 days of the year, large red letters appear: ABCDEFG. These seven letters indicate the days of the week.
modal_calendar.inner: The innermost ring shows the dates of Easter Sundays. Between them are the so-called Golden Numbers, indicating the year's position in the 19-year lunar cycle.
modal_calendar.rule_intro: A Sunday letter (SL) means that all days marked with that letter are Sundays. Monday is the next letter, Tuesday the one after, and so on.
modal_calendar.step2_title: Step 2: Count from SL to DL ⏱️
modal_calendar.step2_text: Start counting at the valid Sunday letter and count forward until the day letter is reached.
modal_calendar.step3_text: The day of the week results from the position in the count (position 0 = Sunday, position 6 = Saturday).
modal_calendar.golden_number_info: After 19 years, the phases of the moon repeat on nearly the same calendar days. The Golden Number plays an important role in calculating the date of Easter and other movable church holidays. Together with other calendrical rules, it helps determine the first full moon after the beginning of spring, on the Sunday following which Easter is celebrated.

modal_history.title: Art & History of the Astronomical Clock 📜
modal_history.headline: The History of the Astronomical Clock 📜
modal_history.intro: The clock in St. Mary's stands in a more than 600-year-old tradition of representation and innovation in the Hanseatic city of Lübeck — from the first tower clock in 1380 to today's structure from 1976.
modal_history.clock0_text: Lübeck's first tower clock with an hour display is built, complemented by four bells in the roof turret — they fall victim to a fire in 1500.
modal_history.clock1_text: The first Astronomical Clock, consisting of a calendar disc and planetarium, is dedicated in the choir ambulatory behind the altar — damaged just two years later by a fire at the altar, but immediately restored. The carved zodiac of this clock survives and can be seen today in the St. Anne's Museum.
modal_history.clock2_text: Clockmaker Matthias van Oß and woodcarver Hinrich Matthes build the second, richly carved Astronomical Clock with calendar disc, planetarium, and the famous Electors' Procession. The work drags on considerably through the plague years of 1564–66. The calendar disc and zodiac from the first clock of 1405 are reused in the process.
modal_history.clock3_text: The Eduard Korfhage tower-clock factory renews the drive, hands, zodiac and calendar disc — the clock receives a new, modern movement.
modal_history.clock4_text: On Palm Sunday, the historic clock is completely destroyed in a bombing raid on Lübeck. Only the parts already relocated to the St. Anne's Museum in 1888/90 — the calendar disc, the zodiac hands of 1405, and further hands and clockwork parts — survive the destruction of their "successors in office".
modal_history.predecessors_special_title: What made the Lübeck clock special
modal_history.predecessors_special_text: Unlike most church clocks, the Lübeck clock displayed not only the sun, moon and zodiac, but also the paths of the five planets known at the time — a wealth of detail matched among Hanseatic church clocks only by the cathedral clock in Münster. Also unique was the recording of visible eclipses, documented since 1563, and a puzzling "gravity clock" on the moon hand whose exact purpose remains uncertain to this day.
modal_history.img_title: 📷 The preserved clockwork in the St. Anne's Museum, Lübeck
modal_history.img_subtitle: Remains of the first Astronomical Clock from 1405 — star disc with gilded figures, gears and hands. The lower wheel is the drive wheel of the clockwork.
modal_history.rebuild1_text: Master clockmaker Paul Behrens (1893–1984), long-serving churchwarden of St. Mary's, begins planning in 1955. He had previously already designed and built the machinery for the new carillon system in the south tower.
modal_history.rebuild2_text: Behrens fundamentally improves the calculation: the old clock worked with a rough 365-day year, accumulating an error of 24 days every 100 years. His new gear ratio of 366¼ to 365¼ days reduces this deviation to just one day per 100 years.
modal_history.rebuild3_text: Gears matching these unusual prime-number ratios could not be bought anywhere — the Lübeck Machine Engineering Company (LMG) manufactured and donated them specially. The new clock is set running for the first time in 1967 and fully completed in 1976.
modal_history.rebuild4_text: Of the mechanisms renewed in 1889/90, only scorched, bent wreckage remained in 1942. Behrens acquired a well-preserved, older tower-clock movement and completely reworked it — including a new hand-drive system and the mechanisms for the hour strike, figure procession, calendar-disc movement, and musical chime.
modal_history.art_intro: The new clock follows the historical three-part division — calendar section, clock dial, figure superstructure — but fundamentally changes what the clock dial actually shows.
modal_history.art_dial_title: Real Constellations Instead of Fixed Signs
modal_history.art_center_text: As before, the figure of the Saviour, emerging from clouds and rays, occupies the centre of the planetarium. Organist H. Jimmerthal, in his 1861 description of the Astronomical Clock, already interpreted this as an allusion to the Gospel of John (John 1:1–4).
modal_history.art_zodiac_text: Almost all astronomical church clocks show an astrological zodiac: twelve equally sized 30-degree segments — as the old Lübeck clock did too. Behrens wanted to depict the actual reality of the stars instead: his 13 constellations (including Ophiuchus, between Scorpio and Sagittarius) are therefore of varying size, just as in the real sky, and some even overlap.
modal_history.art_craft_text: Master joiner Heinrich Brand sawed, engraved and assembled the 13 differently sized constellations so that they hang and rotate on a central axis; a counterweight ensures they always stay upright. Master painter Alfred Mundt carried out the elaborate gold-leaf gilding.
modal_history.art_precession_label: Why astrology and astronomy drift apart:
modal_history.art_precession_text: 2,000 years ago, the sun on March 21st actually stood in the constellation Aries. Due to the slow precession of Earth's axis — one full cycle of the vernal point takes roughly 26,000 years — it in fact still stands in Pisces on the same calendar date today, even though astrology continues to speak of the "sign of Aries". In another 2,000 years, the sun will stand in the constellation Aquarius on March 21st.
modal_history.art_names_text: The zodiac constellations were once simple time markers for recurring events. When Aries and Taurus appeared in the morning sky, it was time to drive the sheep to pasture and yoke the oxen to the plough. Leo, the mightiest animal, stood for the powerful summer sun. Virgo was originally just an ear of grain, marking the start of the harvest — which is why Behrens gave the figure of Virgo an ear of grain to hold again on the new clock. Aquarius is considered the oldest constellation: its early rising once heralded the rainy season.
modal_history.inscription_text: AS OFTEN AS YOU HEAR THE RINGING BELL, DO NOT FORGET YOUR GOD WHO RULES OVER ALL THE STARS, TO PRAISE AND THANK HIM
modal_history.figures_title: The Figure Procession: The Believers of the World
modal_history.fig1_text: Instead of the Electors of the old clock, since 1976 — on the bishop's suggestion — a procession of eight figures of different origins passes before Christ.
modal_history.fig2_text: Unlike before, the figures now move from left to right — because the new clock was also meant to be clearly visible from the nave of the church. This way, the figures visibly walk towards the viewer.
modal_history.fig3_text: Marianne Schmidt designed and made all eight figures, including their artistic painting — down to the smallest detail, such as the ivory-trimmed leather poncho of the Native American figure, carved from a single piece of wood.
modal_history.fig4_text: Above the figure procession, an old man strikes the historic hour bell of 1721 — a gift from the Rotary Club of Ystad. To its left, a female figure with a lowered torch and a skull warns of transience; above it, a double figure — an old man and a young woman — looks as a Janus head simultaneously into past and future. All three figures were faithfully carved from a historical photograph by August Wittich, an 80-year-old woodcarver who had fled Silesia.
modal_history.fig5_text: On the level of the figure procession, Forgiveness (the return of the prodigal son) and Mercy (the Good Samaritan) face one another. Above them follow Humility, Joy, Faith and Love — until Christ, at the very top of the gable, finally embodies Hope.

luebeck_rule.because_before: Since {day}. {month} is before March 1st, the letter {sb} applies.
luebeck_rule.because_after: Since {day}. {month} is after February 28th, the letter {sb} applies.
luebeck_rule.uniform: For the year {year} a uniform Sunday letter applies: {sb}.
